notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Hosea 10, drawn from the allowed sources.

---

## Hosea 10 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### v. 1: *"Israel was a luxuriant vine, yielding fruit for himself…"*

The vine was a standard OT image for Israel (Ps 80:8–11; Isa 5:1–7; Jer 2:21; Ezek 15:1–8). The Hebrew word translated "luxuriant" (or "empty" in the KJV) is debated: it can mean either "degenerate/empty" or "luxuriant/spreading." Ellicott notes that "empty" is wrong and inconsistent with what follows; "luxuriant" is correct. The LXX and Vulgate support "luxuriant." The image is of a wild, strong-growing vine that lavishes fruit — but the fruit is "for himself," not for God. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Gill takes the KJV reading "empty vine" as empty of spiritual fruit, though full of temporal blessings. The fruit they did produce was consumed on their own lusts or on idols. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes the tragedy: Israel used God-given prosperity to build more pagan altars and more elaborate sacred pillars — a warning echoed in Gal 5:13 against using liberty as opportunity for the flesh. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

Precept Austin compiles several teachers: Spurgeon lamented, "It is sad when the more one receives from God, the more one sins." G. Campbell Morgan stressed the pronoun "his": the sin was bearing fruit for self rather than for Jehovah. Robert Chisholm notes the people attributed their success to false gods while maintaining a hypocritical formalism toward Yahweh. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-10-commentary)

The Cambridge Bible: the "fruit" is material, not moral. The prosperity under Jeroboam II only strengthened idolatry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/hosea/10.htm)

---

### v. 2: *"Their hearts are devious; now they must bear their guilt…"*

The Hebrew word *halaq* can mean "divided," "smooth," "flattering," or "slippery." Ellicott says most modern expositors prefer "treacherous (smooth)." The LXX, Raschi, and Aben-Ezra render it "divided." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Guzik notes the wordplay: Israel may have spoken love to God with a smooth, flattering tongue while living a lie — mirroring Gomer's unfaithfulness to Hosea. God would now do in judgment what Israel should have done in contrition: break down the altars. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

Precept Austin notes the fundamental problem was not defective worship but divided allegiance (cf. 1 Ki 18:21; Mt 6:24; Jas 1:8). The phrase "break down their altars" literally means "break the neck of" the altars — God would use the Assyrians as His instrument. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-10-commentary)

Gill sees the divided heart as split between God and idols, or between fellow Israelites through civil discord. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics section notes this divided/smooth heart was the root of the evil: they did not fully devote themselves to God, yet could not part with their idols either. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/hosea/10.htm)

---

### v. 3: *"Surely now they will say, 'We have no king, for we do not revere the LORD. What can a king do for us?'"*

Ellicott sees this as predicting a time of political confusion and helplessness — a vindication of Samuel's warnings in 1 Sam 8:19. As for a king, what will he do for us? — they realize the monarchy is useless when God is against them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Gill suggests this would be said either during the interregnum between Pekah's murder and Hoshea's installment (2 Ki 15:30), or when Samaria was besieged and the king captured. The people finally acknowledge that without fearing the Lord, no human king can help. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary) adds: when destruction came, they would realize that their self-appointed king had failed and no human king could help them. Hoshea would prove to be Israel's last king. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-10.html)

Guzik: "Under the judgment of the LORD, foreign powers dominated Israel so they no longer had their own king." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

---

### v. 4: *"They speak mere words; with false oaths they make covenants. So judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of a field."*

Ellicott says: Divine judgments shall prevail not as a blessing (a precious harvest) but as a curse — a poisonous plant (poppy or hemlock) in the ridges of the field. Their oaths and covenants are empty. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Gill explains: instead of justice being wholesome like a good herb, it sprang up like hemlock — bitter and poisonous — spreading through the whole kingdom. They belched out "oaths of vanity." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

Guzik: "judgment springs up like hemlock in the furrows of the field" — the image is of poisonous weeds overtaking what should have been a fruitful crop. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

---

### v. 5: *"The people of Samaria will fear for the calf of Beth-aven… its idolatrous priests…"*

Ellicott highlights the "sarcastic force and concentrated scoff" of the Hebrew: "calves" is literally *she-calves* — the feminine form expresses contempt. The word for "priests" (*kemarîm*) always designates an idolatrous priesthood. Beth-aven ("house of iniquity") is a scornful renaming of Bethel ("house of God"). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Gill likewise notes the contempt: "cow calves" — denoting their weakness and inability to help. The priests (*Chemarim*, meaning "black ones") would mourn because their livelihood was taken. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

Constable: Beth-aven may stand not merely for Bethel but for the whole official, semi-pagan religious setup in Israel. The idolatrous priests (*kemarim*, cf. 2 Ki 23:5; Zeph 1:4) would bewail the demise of the altar. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-10.html)

---

### v. 6: *"Yes, it will be carried to Assyria as tribute to the great king…"*

The "it" is the golden calf itself. Ellicott: "Even that (i.e., the calf) shall be carried (in triumphant state) to Assyria, an offering to King Jareb." For "King Jareb," see Hosea 5:13 — the name may mean "King Pick-Quarrel" or "the contentious king," likely referring to the Assyrian monarch. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Gill: the calf, being all of gold, would be plundered and sent as a present to the Assyrian king. Ephraim would be ashamed both of worshipping an idol that could not save itself, and of their political counsel in making alliances. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

Guzik: "Even the idols they honored and trusted so much will be taken to foreign lands as treasure for foreign kings." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

---

### v. 7: *"Samaria will be carried off with her king like a twig on the surface of the water."*

Ellicott calls this "one of the most striking images in the prophecy." The Hebrew *qetseph* means "chip" or "fragment," not "foam" — "like a chip on the waters' surface," carried helplessly by the current. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Gill: like foam or a bubble — something that appears substantial but is suddenly and easily destroyed. Kings and kingdoms are mere bubbles, "swell, look big and high for a while," then vanish. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

Guzik: the king of Samaria is "cut off," swept away helplessly like a twig on fast-moving water. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

---

### v. 8: *"The high places of Aven will be destroyed… Then they will say to the mountains, 'Cover us!' and to the hills, 'Fall on us!'"*

"Aven" (meaning "iniquity") is a further scornful shortening of Beth-aven/Bethel. Gill: the high places — the temple and altars for idolatry — would be demolished. Thorns and thistles would overgrow the ruined altars. The people, in despair, would call on the very mountains where they committed idolatry to hide them from God's wrath. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

Guzik notes that Jesus quotes this verse in Luke 23:30 (on the way to the cross), and it appears again in Rev 6:16 (the sixth seal) — it becomes a cry of those facing divine judgment who prefer sudden death to protracted suffering. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

Precept Austin (Cyril Hocking): "The Assyrian would come and strip them. Despair would be theirs and they would cry for sudden death rather than endure protracted captivity." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-10-commentary)

Gaebelein connects this to Christ's words about Jerusalem's judgment and the sixth seal in Revelation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/hosea-10.html)

---

### v. 9: *"Since the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel, and there you have remained…"*

This refers to the horrific events of Judges 19–20 (the Levite's concubine, the civil war with Benjamin). Ellicott: Gibeah is "emblematic of gross and cruel sensuality," just as Sodom is for unnatural vice. The phrase "there they stood" means they remained sinning in the same manner. The question "Did not the battle in Gibeah overtake the sons of iniquity?" may be read as: shall there not overtake them a war like the one against Gibeah? (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Gill notes two interpretations: either Israel's sins were not new — they were the same as those at Gibeah long ago — or Israel had sinned *more* than in the days of Gibeah. The battle at Gibeah did not destroy the Benjamites completely (600 escaped), but the coming judgment would be total. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

Guzik: Gibeah was already mentioned in Hosea 9:9. Even though a battle was fought against the "children of iniquity" there, iniquity persisted in Israel. God wanted willfully blind Israel to see their sin. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

---

### v. 10: *"I will chasten them when I please; nations will be gathered against them to put them in bondage for their double transgression."*

Ellicott: "When I desire, I will chastise them" — God acts at His own sovereign timing. The "two iniquities" refer to the two calves at Bethel and Dan, the source of heresy and treason against Jehovah. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Constable offers two main views: (1) the double guilt is original sin at Gibeah plus present sin at Bethel; (2) the sin of forsaking God and the sin of forsaking His appointed Davidic kings. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-10.html)

Precept Austin suggests the first sin was idolatry and the second was the stubborn refusal to repent — making a bad situation worse. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-10-commentary)

Gill notes the marginal reading (*Keri*) is "their two iniquities," which the LXX and Vulgate follow — interpreting it as the two calves, or corporeal and spiritual adultery. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

---

### v. 11: *"Ephraim is a well-trained heifer that loves to thresh; but I will place a yoke on her fair neck…"*

Ellicott explains: threshing was relatively easy, pleasant work — the ox could eat freely as it trod out the grain (Deut 25:4). Ephraim loved this easy, self-indulgent life. But God would "pass by the fairness of her neck" — arresting her self-indulgence — and harness her for the hard labor of plowing. "I will harness Ephraim for riding" means a rider (Assyria) would take possession. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Gill: Ephraim loved freedom and ease, like an unmuzzled heifer treading corn. But now they would be yoked in hard service — Judah would plow, Jacob would break clods — all under harsh foreign domination. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

Guzik: Like unruly farm animals, God would control and guide Israel even if they kicked against Him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

The Expositor's Bible Commentary: "It is all very well for the unmuzzled beast to love the threshing, but harder and unrewarded labors of ploughing and harrowing have to come before the floor be heaped with sheaves. Israel must not expect religious festival without religious discipline." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/hosea-10.html)

---

### v. 12: *"Sow for yourselves righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion; break up your unplowed ground…"*

This is the key verse of the chapter — a call to repentance amid judgment. Ellicott: "In their despair come some characteristic gleams of hope on the desolation; the eternal law which makes reaping a consequence of sowing will still apply." The soil of the soul is fallow and unbroken. Break it up, seek Jehovah, and He will come "as never before." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Derek Kidner (quoted by Precept Austin): "The one gleam of light, the invitation of Hosea 10:12, is the *raison d'être* of the whole chapter." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-10-commentary)

Guzik: Fallow ground hasn't been plowed for more than a year — it's hard, stubborn, and resistant. It doesn't "want" to be broken up; the plow hurts. Yet it's useless as long as it remains fallow. The call "For it is time to seek the LORD" means *now* — "the season is passing." Breaking up fallow ground is done by seeking the LORD, not self or idols. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

Constable: Breaking up fallow ground figures confessing sins long unconfessed under the surface of life. This verse "is a good summary of what all Israel's prophets appealed to God's people to do throughout their history (cf. 2 Cor 6:2)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-10.html)

F.B. Meyer: "Is it not time that we should look into our hearts and lives, break up the fallow ground, now covered with thorns and thistles, and begin to sow in righteousness?" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/hosea-10.html)

---

### v. 13: *"You have plowed wickedness and reaped injustice; you have eaten the fruit of lies. Because you have trusted in your own way…"*

Ellicott notes a textual variant: the Hebrew for "thy way" (*darkeka*) could, with a slight change, read "thy chariots" — a reading followed by the LXX, Ewald, and others. This would create a good parallelism with "multitude of mighty men." But the Masoretic text gives "a fine meaning": trusting in one's own path rather than God's. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Guzik: "Because you trusted in your own way: This is the essence of all sin. We trust in our own way instead of in God's way. Ruin always comes when we trust in our own way." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

Constable: instead of plowing righteousness and reaping *hesed* (loving devotion, v. 12), they plowed wickedness and reaped injustice — trusting in military might rather than Yahweh. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-10.html)

---

### v. 14: *"the roar of battle will rise against your people… as Shalman devastated Beth-arbel… when mothers were dashed to pieces along with their children."*

The identity of Shalman and Beth-arbel is uncertain. Ellicott: "The prophet seems to hear the advance of the invading army, and see the fall of Samaria's fortress." No consensus exists on the historical event — it was evidently a well-known atrocity in Hosea's day. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

Gaebelein identifies Shalman as a contracted form of Shalmanezer, the King of Assyria. There is no further biblical record of Beth-arbel's destruction; it was a known event that needed no explanation for Hosea's audience. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/hosea-10.html)

Constable notes the same uncertainty and says it was "one in Israel's past, but what past event is uncertain." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-10.html)

Gill: the horrific detail of mothers dashed upon their children describes the brutality of ancient siege warfare — an image of total devastation. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

---

### v. 15: *"Thus it will be done to you, O Bethel, because of your great wickedness. When the day dawns, the king of Israel will be utterly cut off."*

Gaebelein: Bethel was the seat of Israel's idolatry; it drew God's wrath and "finally ended the monarchy in Israel and their national existence." The phrase "at dawn" suggests the swiftness and suddenness of judgment — the king would be "cut off utterly" in the morning, when a new day might have been expected. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/hosea-10.html)

Guzik: Bethel ("house of God") is addressed directly as the center of false worship. The dawn brings not hope but final judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

---

## Protestant Traditions: Points of Differing Emphasis

Given the available sources, here are the distinct emphases that emerged:

**Reformed / Puritan (Matthew Henry, Spurgeon):** Strong emphasis on the sovereign "heart" issue. Henry (quoted at Precept Austin): "God is the Sovereign of the heart; he will have all, or none." The divided heart is the root — outward idolatry is symptom. Spurgeon stressed the tragedy of prosperity leading to sin: the richer the land, the more they sinned. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-10-commentary)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Strong emphasis on personal application. The call to "break up your fallow ground" is framed as an urgent, personal, now-word: "The time to break up the fallow ground is now… the season is passing." Guzik draws direct parallels to the Christian life (Gal 5:13; sowing and reaping in the believer's walk). The Hebrew word study on *halaq* (divided/smooth/flattering) is used to highlight insincere worship. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-10/)

**Baptist (Gill):** Careful attention to alternative readings and translation issues. Gill treats the KJV "empty vine" seriously, interpreting it as emptiness of spiritual fruit. He gives detailed attention to historical context (the interregnum between Pekah and Hoshea, Jewish traditions about the calves being taken). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/10.htm)

**Dispensational (Gaebelein, Constable):** Gaebelein sees the chapter as part of a larger structure in which Hosea 10:12–15 is the "exhortation and rebuke" section before Hosea 11's message of mercy. He connects v. 8 directly to the yet-future judgment in Revelation. Constable (Dallas Seminary) emphasizes the historical-political context: Hoshea as Israel's last king, Assyrian foreign policy, the double guilt as possibly forsaking Davidic kings. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/hosea-10.html, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/hosea-10.html)

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott gives careful, scholarly attention to the Hebrew text and translation issues (e.g., "empty" vs. "luxuriant," *qetseph* as "chip" not "foam," the feminine plural "she-calves" for contempt). He notes where the LXX reading differs. His tone is measured and exegetical, not strongly hortatory. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)

---

## Other Views: Where Available

**NET Bible notes:** The NET Bible translates *halaq* as "slipping" ("Their heart is slipping") and supplies "to Baal" in v. 1 for clarity, though it does not appear in the Hebrew. The NET text notes that the phrase "to Baal" is implied but not in the original. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-10-commentary — NET translation quoted under v. 1)

**LXX / Septuagint readings:** The LXX renders the Hebrew as "a vine with goodly branches" (flourishing), not "empty." In v. 13, the LXX reads "chariots" instead of "way," which some modern scholars (Ewald, Nowack) prefer. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/10.htm)
